list_database_accounts.title: List Cosmos DB accounts in the subscription
list_database_accounts.description: Every Cosmos DB account in the subscription, with its API kind (GlobalDocumentDB for NoSQL, MongoDB, Parse), consistency policy, the regions it is replicated to, and its `documentEndpoint` -- the host the `azure-cosmos-db` data-plane connector needs.

output.description: Every Cosmos DB account in the subscription.

items.description: id, name, location, kind and properties (documentEndpoint, consistencyPolicy, locations, enableMultipleWriteLocations, capabilities, provisioningState).

list_database_accounts_in_group.title: List Cosmos DB accounts in a resource group
list_database_accounts_in_group.description: The Cosmos DB accounts in one resource group, with the same detail as list_database_accounts. Cheaper when the group is known.

resource_group.description: The resource group to look in.

items.description: id, name, location, kind and properties.

get_database_account.title: Get a Cosmos DB account
get_database_account.description:
One account in full: its default consistency level, every region it is replicated to with that region's failover priority, whether multi-region writes are on, its capabilities (`EnableServerless`, `EnableNoSQLVectorSearch` and so on), backup policy, and network rules.
`capabilities` is worth reading before anything else -- a serverless account cannot have throughput provisioned, and several features are capabilities that must be enabled at the account rather than per container.

properties.description: documentEndpoint, consistencyPolicy, locations, readLocations, writeLocations, enableMultipleWriteLocations, capabilities, backupPolicy, ipRules and provisioningState.

create_or_update_database_account.title: Create or update a Cosmos DB account
create_or_update_database_account.description:
Create a Cosmos DB account or change an existing one's configuration. The name becomes part of a public DNS name and is globally unique.
Three decisions here are effectively permanent: the API `kind` (GlobalDocumentDB for NoSQL, MongoDB for the Mongo wire protocol), whether the account is serverless (a capability, not a flag you can toggle later), and the account's original write region.
`locations` is the full replication list -- each entry a `{"locationName": "...", "failoverPriority": 0}` -- and it REPLACES the current set, so removing a region from it removes that replica. Creation and region changes are asynchronous and can take many minutes.
create_or_update_database_account.notes: The API kind and serverless capability cannot be changed after creation. `locations` replaces the whole replication set.

resource_group.description: The resource group to create the account in.

account_name.description: The account name -- globally unique, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens.

location.description: The account's primary region, in wire form.

locations.description: The full replication set, each entry {"locationName": "westeurope", "failoverPriority": 0}. Priority 0 is the write region. This replaces the current set.

kind.description: The account API. GlobalDocumentDB is the NoSQL API. Fixed at creation.

default_consistency_level.description: Session is the usual default. Strong costs more and restricts multi-region writes; Eventual is cheapest and weakest.

max_staleness_interval_seconds.description: For BoundedStaleness, how many seconds a read may lag.

max_staleness_prefix.description: For BoundedStaleness, how many operations a read may lag.

enable_multiple_write_locations.description: Allow writes in every region. Changes conflict handling and cost.

enable_automatic_failover.description: Let Azure fail the write region over automatically during a regional outage.

capabilities.description: Account capabilities, each {"name": "EnableServerless"} or {"name": "EnableNoSQLVectorSearch"}. Serverless cannot be added later.

public_network_access.description: Disabled restricts the account to private endpoints.

output.description: The account as created or updated; provisioning continues asynchronously.

delete_database_account.title: Delete a Cosmos DB account
delete_database_account.description:
Destroy a Cosmos DB account, every database and container in it, and every document. Whether anything can be recovered depends entirely on the account's backup policy having been Continuous rather than Periodic -- check get_database_account's `backupPolicy` first, because with Periodic backup a restore needs a support request and the account's own restore window.
Asynchronous and, for practical purposes, final.
delete_database_account.notes: Destroys all data. Recovery depends on the backup policy configured beforehand.

list_account_keys.title: Get a Cosmos DB account's master keys
list_account_keys.description:
The account's primary and secondary master keys, plus the read-only pair. A master key is unrestricted read-write access to every database and document in the account, never expires and cannot be scoped down, so the response is a credential and must be treated as one.
Prefer Entra ID with a Cosmos DB data-plane role -- which is what the `azure-cosmos-db` connector uses -- and reach for keys only when something cannot do that.
list_account_keys.notes: Returns live credentials granting full access to all data in the account. Do not log the output.

secondaryMasterKey.description: The rotation partner of the primary. Secret.

list_read_only_keys.title: Get a Cosmos DB account's read-only keys
list_read_only_keys.description: Only the two read-only master keys, which grant reads across the whole account and no writes. Narrower than list_account_keys and the right choice for anything that only queries -- still a credential, still unexpiring, still unscoped to a database.
list_read_only_keys.notes: Returns live read credentials for the whole account.

list_connection_strings.title: Get a Cosmos DB account's connection strings
list_connection_strings.description: Ready-made connection strings for the account, one per key and per supported protocol -- which is what a MongoDB or Cassandra driver wants rather than a bare key. Each embeds a master key, so the whole response is a credential.
list_connection_strings.notes: Each string embeds a master key. Treat the response as secret.

items.description: connectionString and description (Primary/Secondary, read-write or read-only).

regenerate_account_key.title: Rotate a Cosmos DB master key
regenerate_account_key.description: Replace one of the account's four keys. Everything still using the old value STOPS WORKING IMMEDIATELY. The pairs exist so you can move consumers to the secondary, rotate the primary, and move back -- rotating both at once is an outage.
regenerate_account_key.notes: Immediately invalidates the old key value.

output.description: Empty on acceptance; the rotation completes asynchronously.

update_failover_priority.title: Change which region a Cosmos DB account writes to
update_failover_priority.description:
Reorder the account's regions by failover priority. The region at priority 0 is the write region, so changing that PERFORMS A FAILOVER on a single-write-region account -- writes move, and in-flight ones can fail.
Every region the account is replicated to must appear in the list exactly once. This is the manual counterpart of `enableAutomaticFailover`; use it for a planned regional move or a drill, not casually.
update_failover_priority.notes: Changing the priority-0 region moves the write region, which is a real failover.

failover_policies.description: Every region with its new priority, each {"locationName": "northeurope", "failoverPriority": 0}. Priority 0 is the write region.

output.description: Empty on acceptance; the failover runs asynchronously.

list_sql_databases.title: List the SQL (NoSQL) databases in an account
list_sql_databases.description: Every database in a NoSQL-API Cosmos DB account. Databases are just namespaces for containers; the data and most of the cost live one level down. Only meaningful on accounts whose `kind` is GlobalDocumentDB.

create_sql_database.title: Create a SQL (NoSQL) database
create_sql_database.description:
Create a database in a NoSQL-API account. Optionally give it shared throughput, which every container in it then draws from -- cheaper than provisioning each container separately when they are individually small, but they compete with one another under load.
Leave both throughput arguments off on a serverless account, which cannot have throughput provisioned at all.
create_sql_database.notes: Provisioned throughput starts billing as soon as the database exists, whether or not anything uses it.

throughput.description: Manual shared throughput in RU/s for the whole database, minimum 400. Mutually exclusive with max_autoscale_throughput.

max_autoscale_throughput.description: Autoscale ceiling in RU/s; the database scales between a tenth of this and this. Minimum 1000.

delete_sql_database.title: Delete a SQL (NoSQL) database
delete_sql_database.description: Destroy a database and every container and document in it. Irreversible unless the account has continuous backup configured, in which case a restore is a separate account-level operation.

database_name.description: The database to destroy, with everything in it.

list_sql_containers.title: List the containers in a Cosmos DB database
list_sql_containers.description: Every container in a database, with its partition key paths, indexing policy, unique key policy, default TTL and conflict resolution policy. The partition key is the single most consequential thing about a container and cannot be changed after creation, so this is worth reading before designing a query.

items.description: id, name and properties.resource (id, partitionKey, indexingPolicy, uniqueKeyPolicy, defaultTtl, conflictResolutionPolicy).

get_sql_container.title: Get a Cosmos DB container
get_sql_container.description: One container's definition: its partition key path and kind, its indexing policy including any vector or composite indexes, its unique key policy and its default TTL. `defaultTtl` is the one that quietly deletes documents -- a positive value means every document expires that many seconds after its last write unless it overrides it.

create_sql_container.title: Create a Cosmos DB container
create_sql_container.description:
Create a container in a database. The `partition_key_paths` decision is permanent and determines how the container scales -- pick a property with high cardinality and even access, such as `/tenantId` or `/userId`, not something with a handful of values.
Throughput can be provisioned here (manual or autoscale) or inherited from the database if that has shared throughput. Serverless accounts take neither.
`default_ttl` set to a positive number expires every document that many seconds after its last write; -1 enables TTL but expires nothing unless a document sets its own.
create_sql_container.notes: The partition key cannot be changed after creation. Provisioned throughput bills from creation.

database_name.description: The database to create the container in.

partition_key_paths.description: Partition key paths, e.g. ["/tenantId"]. Permanent. More than one path makes a hierarchical partition key.

partition_key_kind.description: Hash for a normal key, MultiHash for a hierarchical one.

default_ttl.description: Seconds after last write before a document expires. -1 enables TTL without a default. Omit to disable expiry entirely.

indexing_policy.description: The indexing policy -- includedPaths, excludedPaths, compositeIndexes, vectorIndexes. Omit for Cosmos DB's index-everything default.

unique_key_policy.description: Unique constraints within a partition, as {"uniqueKeys": [{"paths": ["/email"]}]}. Permanent.

throughput.description: Manual throughput in RU/s for this container, minimum 400.

delete_sql_container.title: Delete a Cosmos DB container
delete_sql_container.description: Destroy a container and every document in it, along with any throughput provisioned on it. Irreversible unless the account has continuous backup. The database and its other containers are unaffected.

container_name.description: The container to destroy, with every document in it.

get_sql_database_throughput.title: Get a database's shared throughput
get_sql_database_throughput.description: The RU/s provisioned at database level, shared by every container in it. `throughput` is a manual setting; `autoscaleSettings.maxThroughput` means autoscale, in which case the account bills between a tenth of that and that. A 404 means the database has no shared throughput -- either its containers are provisioned individually, or the account is serverless.

output.description: The database's throughput settings, or 404 when it has none.

get_sql_container_throughput.title: Get a container's throughput
get_sql_container_throughput.description: The RU/s provisioned on one container, manual or autoscale, along with `minimumThroughput` -- the floor you cannot scale below, which grows with the data stored and with the highest throughput the container has ever had. That floor is why a container sometimes will not scale back down as far as it started.

output.description: The container's throughput settings, or 404 when it inherits the database's.

update_sql_container_throughput.title: Change a container's throughput
update_sql_container_throughput.description:
Set the RU/s on a container -- manual with `throughput`, or an autoscale ceiling with `max_autoscale_throughput`. This is the direct cost lever: provisioned RU/s bill continuously whether or not anything queries the container.
Raising throughput takes effect quickly. Lowering it is bounded by `minimumThroughput` from get_sql_container_throughput, and a request below that floor is rejected rather than clamped.
update_sql_container_throughput.notes: Changes the bill immediately. Lowering is bounded by the container's minimumThroughput.

throughput.description: Manual RU/s. Use this or max_autoscale_throughput, not both.

max_autoscale_throughput.description: Autoscale ceiling in RU/s. The container scales between a tenth of this and this.

output.description: The throughput settings after the change.

list_sql_role_definitions.title: List Cosmos DB data-plane role definitions
list_sql_role_definitions.description: The data-plane roles defined on the account -- the built-in Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader and Data Contributor, plus any custom ones -- each with the data actions it permits. These are what make Entra ID access possible without master keys, and they are completely separate from Azure RBAC's control-plane roles.

items.description: id, name and properties (roleName, type, assignableScopes, permissions.dataActions).

list_sql_role_assignments.title: List Cosmos DB data-plane role assignments
list_sql_role_assignments.description: Which Entra ID principals hold which data-plane role over which scope of the account. This is the answer to "why can this service principal read documents" -- and to why one cannot, when it has Contributor on the account in Azure RBAC but no data-plane assignment here. Those are different systems and control-plane roles grant no data access.

items.description: id, name and properties (roleDefinitionId, principalId, scope).
